  "core_problem": "Process reward models face a fundamental accuracy-cost trade-off at the step level: discriminative (fast scalar) verification is cheap (~10ms/step) but unreliable on hard reasoning steps, while generative (CoT) verification is far more accurate but ~100-500x more expensive (~1-5s/step). (2) F/S-RM (Mar 2026) proves a single model can support both discriminative and generative modes with dual-confidence routing → provides the architectural foundation. (4) CoT Entropy (arXiv 2502.11250) achieves best-in-class step-level uncertainty quantification for generative PRMs (AUROC 0.680) → provides validated signal for criticality estimation. (5) Constrained GRPO (arXiv 2602.05863) and Faithful GRPO (arXiv 2604.08476) provide principled frameworks for enforcing quality constraints during RL training → enables the F1 floor guarantee. Pattern: 'Dyve showed the right question (adaptive step verification) and demonstrated its value. The next step requires explicit routing that composes with stronger base models, principled criticality estimation, and constrained training with quality guarantees.'",
  "approach": "We propose CRISP-PRM (CRIticality-based Step-level Paradigm selection for Process Reward Models), a framework built on a unified dual-mode verifier that selects the verification paradigm—fast (discriminative) or deep (generative CoT)—for each reasoning step based on estimated step criticality, under a compute budget constraint. Building on Dyve's pioneering demonstration that step-level paradigm selection outperforms contemporaneous baselines, CRISP-PRM introduces explicit, composable routing designed to work with modern strong base models.\n\n**Architecture: Unified Dual-Mode PRM**\n\nCRISP-PRM uses a single Qwen3-8B model fine-tuned to support both verification modes, following the F/S-RM dual-mode paradigm adapted for step-level process verification:\n\n• Fast mode: Given (problem, solution prefix, step_i), the model's first generated token is a correctness judgment ('correct'/'incorrect'). The token probability p(correct|context) serves directly as a scalar step reward. Cost: ~10ms/step (single forward pass). No separate classification head needed—the standard LM head suffices.\n\n• Deep mode: A special trigger token is appended to the prompt, bypassing fast judgment and entering CoT verification. The model generates a step-by-step verification rationale inside <verify>...</verify> tags, then outputs a final correctness judgment. Cost: ~100ms-2s/step depending on model size and generation length.\n\n**Training Pipeline: Two-Stage with Constrained RL**\n\nStage 1 — SFT Foundation: Combined loss L = L_step + λ·L_action, where L_step is binary cross-entropy on step labels (fast mode) combined with generation loss on synthetic verification CoTs from ThinkPRM-style data (deep mode), and L_action is an action-space constraint penalizing probability leakage to irrelevant tokens during fast mode.\n\nStage 2 — Constrained GRPO with F1 Floor: We adopt the Constrained GRPO framework (arXiv 2602.05863) to fine-tune the unified model with a hard F1 floor guarantee—ensuring the model never degrades below the discriminative baseline quality. Concrete specification:\n\n(a) Indicator cost function: C_F1(π) = 𝕀[F1_batch(π) < F1_threshold], where F1_threshold is set to the discriminative baseline F1 on a held-out ProcessBench validation split (avg F1 73.5 for Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B class models).\n\n(b) Lagrangian objective: ℒ(π,λ) = J_R(π) − λ·(J_C(π) − d̃), where J_R is the primary reward (format correctness + outcome accuracy for both fast and deep modes), J_C is the constraint violation rate, and d̃ is the target violation rate (0.05 = at most 5% of validation batches may fall below F1_threshold).\n\n(c) Scalarized advantage construction (NOT scalarized rewards, following arXiv 2602.05863 Theorem 4.1 to prevent standard-deviation mismatch): A_ScAdv = λ_R·Z_R − λ_C·Z_C, where Z_j = (Component_j − mean(Component_j))/std(Component_j) are per-component standardized advantages. This preserves the intended trade-off between reward maximization and constraint satisfaction.\n\n(d) Multiplier update: ∇_λ ℒ = −(J_C(π) − d̃), applied via gradient descent with projection λ ≥ 0. When F1 drops below threshold (J_C > d̃), the gradient is positive, increasing λ and strengthening the constraint penalty.\n\n(e) Conservative checkpoint selection as fallback: evaluate F1 on validation set per epoch; only accept parameter updates that maintain F1 above threshold. This provides a hard guarantee even if the Lagrangian balance oscillates during training.\n\nThis follows the precedent of Faithful GRPO (arXiv 2604.08476), which demonstrated that transforming quality metrics from reward terms into hard constraints via Lagrangian dual ascent reduces quality degradation from 24.5% to 1.7%.\n\n**Step Criticality Estimator (SCE)**\n\nA lightweight module (<1M params) that scores each step's need for deep verification using multiple complementary signals. Unlike Dyve's implicit routing (where the model learns to self-regulate output length through SFT, with no separable routing component), the SCE is an explicit, interpretable, and ablatable module.\n\nThe SCE combines:\n1. Fast-mode intuition confidence: C_I = |p(correct) − p(incorrect)| from the fast verification pass (available as a byproduct)\n2. Fast-mode token confidence: C_T = mean negative log-probability of irrelevant tokens, measuring probability mass leakage beyond the binary judgment (from F/S-RM's dual-confidence mechanism)\n3. CoT Entropy signal: Following Ye et al. (arXiv 2502.11250), when running complementary analysis, sample multiple reasoning paths at each step and compute entropy over the marginal distribution of binary decision outcomes: H = −Σ_e(Σ_c p_θ(c,e|x≤t)) log(Σ_c p_θ(c,e|x≤t)). Steps with high CoT Entropy indicate verifier uncertainty requiring deeper analysis. Optional when compute-constrained.\n4. Generator internal uncertainty: entropy of the generating model's hidden states via ReProbe-style probes (<10M params on frozen generator), when generator internals are available. Optional for black-box generator settings.\n5. Structural features: step position in chain, relative token length, domain signal. Justified by CoLD (arXiv 2507.15698) showing PRMs have strong length bias.\n\nThe SCE is an MLP that outputs a criticality score c_i ∈ [0,1] for each step. Training signal derives from oracle construction: run both fast and deep modes on training steps, identify 'value-add' steps where fast mode misclassifies but deep mode succeeds, and train SCE via binary cross-entropy. We include a planned ablation ladder: (i) fast-mode confidence only → (ii) dual-confidence (C_I + C_T) → (iii) +CoT Entropy → (iv) +ReProbe → (v) +structural features.\n\n**Budget-Constrained Router**\n\nGiven a per-solution compute budget B (fraction of steps receiving deep verification), the router:\n1. Runs fast verification on ALL K steps (cheap baseline, ~60ms for 6 steps). This simultaneously produces scalar scores and SCE input signals.\n2. Computes criticality scores c_i for all steps.\n3. Selects the top-⌈B·K⌉ highest-criticality steps for deep verification.\n4. Final step scores combine fast and deep assessments: steps receiving only fast verification use the fast scalar score; steps receiving deep verification use the deep judgment.\n\nThe budget B is a tunable hyperparameter that parameterizes the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier: at B=0, all steps use fast verification (cheapest); at B=1, all steps use deep verification (most accurate). The SCE threshold mapping to a given B is calibrated from the empirical criticality score distribution on a calibration set. Critically, the cost ratio between paradigms enters ONLY through B—as generative costs decrease, B can be increased to allocate more deep verification at the same total cost.\n\n**Sequential Error Cascade (SEC) Enhancement (Optional)**\n\nFor applications where step ordering matters, we add a sequential processing mode grounded in CRM's multiplicative survival decomposition and PURE's min-form insight:\n- If deep verification detects an ERROR at step i: automatically flag all subsequent steps for deep verification or assign minimum scores (since they are built on faulty premises).\n- If deep verification CONFIRMS correctness: update posterior criticality of subsequent steps, potentially lowering priority for dependent downstream steps.\nThis is an optional enhancement that provides marginal accuracy gains on top of the core budget-constrained routing.\n\n**Robustness to Cheaper Generative Verification**\n\nCRISP-PRM's value proposition is robust to future reductions in generative verification cost, for six reasons: (a) Even a 10x speedup in generative models leaves a 10-50x cost gap (100-500ms vs 10ms per step)—routing still provides substantial efficiency gains. (b) The SCE provides accuracy gains independent of cost: by identifying which steps most benefit from deeper analysis, routing improves verification allocation quality regardless of per-mode costs. Even at equal costs, selectively applying deep verification to high-criticality steps outperforms uniform application because the model's deep mode may still outperform its fast mode on specific error types (e.g., soundness errors, multi-step logical chains). (c) CRISP-PRM's routing is parameterizable—the cost ratio enters only through the budget constraint B and SCE threshold, both tunable hyperparameters. As costs converge, B increases to allocate more deep verification while maintaining cost parity with uniform fast. (d) In the limit where generative cost equals discriminative cost, CRISP-PRM degenerates to uniform deep verification, which is the accuracy-optimal baseline—the framework gracefully adapts rather than becoming irrelevant. (e) Historical analog: TRIM (arXiv 2601.10245) shows step-level routing between models of different sizes remains valuable even as smaller models improve, because the relative cost gap persists across model generations. (f) GenPRM-1.5B still requires multiple forward passes for CoT generation—the cost gap is fundamental (single-token vs multi-token generation) rather than purely model-size dependent.\n\n**Difficulty-Stratified Efficiency Analysis**\n\nUsing ProcessBench data (arXiv 2412.06559, ACL 2025; verified in R-PRM, arXiv 2503.21295, EMNLP 2025, Table 1) for Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B: err accuracy of 72.0%/68.0%/55.7%/55.2% and corr accuracy of 96.4%/90.4%/85.5%/83.0% across GSM8K/MATH/OlympiadBench/OmniMATH. The fraction of steps where deep verification adds value scales with difficulty:\n\n• Easy tier (GSM8K-level): Fast verification reliable on ~85-90% of steps. Deep needed on ~10-15%. Expected latency reduction vs uniform deep: ~87%.\n• Medium tier (MATH-level): Fast verification reliable on ~80-85% of steps. Deep needed on ~15-20%.
